title: Reconsidering the term ‘deep sea’
content:
Abstract
The term ‘deep sea’, which is often interchangeable with the term ‘deep ocean’, relies on the definition of the global ocean deeper than 200 m, often with the caveat of being beyond the continental shelf, and/or corresponding to other abiotic factors. The general perception and perceived value of large swaths of the marine environment can be altered, positively or negatively depending on context, using the simple prefix of ‘deep-sea’. This paper scrutinizes the 200 m depth contour as a subjective term that originated over 150 years ago in the North Atlantic region at a time when Western open ocean marine science was first developing. As such, this depth correlates with the depth of the North Atlantic continental shelf and holds little relevance elsewhere. Nor does it consistently reflect boundaries in environmental parameters such as light penetration, water mass stratification, or food supply. Furthermore, many examples of ‘shallow’ taxa extending far beyond this depth, ‘deep’ taxa ascending above it, and other taxa that are neither ‘shallow’ nor ‘deep’ (as defined by 200 m) illustrate the 200 m isobath is not consistently biologically limiting. Additionally, as technology has evolved, we are now regularly fishing, consuming, damaging, and drilling at depths far beyond 200 m, demonstrating that what was once considered ‘deep’ is now within routine human reach. In the interest of progressing deep-ocean science and how we communicate it effectively, we question the validity and, by extension, usefulness of 200 m as a boundary between shallow and deep, which oversimplifies complex environmental and biological gradients. Aligning with historical progression in scientific ideas, we argue for gradient-based approaches that more accurately capture spatial heterogeneity and functional transitions across depth, rather than relying on the rigid binary classification term of deep sea.
